newsitem.title: USA: California voters defeat managed care reform measures.
newsitem.headline: California voters defeat managed care reform measures.

text.p: Voters in California defeated two ballot initiatives that would have made it harder for health maintenance organizations to deny patients care.

Propositions 214 and 216, the state's "Health Care Consumer Protection" initiatives had been watched closely outside of California as a sign of how much the rapidly-growing managed health care system could be regulated.

Both measures would have barred HMOs from offering doctors financial incentives to deny patients care, and would have given patients the right to a second opinion before they were refused a drug or treatment.

Proposition 216 also would have taxed HMO executives earning $2.5 million a year, imposed a one-percent tax on mergers of managed care companies, and set up a nonprofit consumer watchdog group to monitor HMOs.

"Californians have said NO to more government involvement in health care," Duane Dauner, president of the California Healthcare Association said in a statement after polls showed the measures being defeated overwhelmingly.

Backers of the measures, however, said they were outspent 20 to 1 in television advertising by the HMOs, who raised the specter of higher taxes and used the confusion over the two competing reform measures to their favor.
